The validate Middleware

A closure that turns any Zod schema into Express middleware — the same shape as asyncHandler.

safeParse (previous slide) is generic — it knows nothing about Express, req, or res. middleware/validate.js is what bridges the two: it takes a schema (or a small map of them) and returns an actual Express middleware function.

// Figure 3.5: turning a Zod schema into middleware (src/middleware/validate.js)
const REQUEST_PARTS = ['params', 'query', 'body'];

export default (schemas) =>
  (req, res, next) => {
    for (const part of REQUEST_PARTS) {
      const schema = schemas[part];
      if (!schema) continue;

      const result = schema.safeParse(req[part]);
      if (!result.success) {
        const details = result.error.issues.map((issue) => ({
          field: issue.path.join('.') || part,
          message: issue.message,
        }));
        return next(new ApiError(400, 'Validation failed', details));
      }

      req[part] = result.data;
    }

    next();
  };

This is the exact same (a) => (b) => ... shape as asyncHandler (Lesson 1, Figure 1.10): calling validate({ body: someSchema }) doesn't run any validation itself — it returns a new function, closing over schemas, and that function is what Express actually calls on every matching request. One call to validate(...) per route, at the point that route is defined; the validation work happens later, once per request.

Inside, it loops over whichever of params/query/body the caller actually supplied a schema for — a route with nothing to validate in the query string, say, simply never passes a query key, and that part of the loop is skipped entirely. ApiError (previous topic, Figure 3.2) is how a validation failure gets to the centralized error handler with a 400 status and a field-by-field details list attached, the same route every other error in this API already takes (Lesson 1's centralized error handling).
